articles.title: Gonzalo Bernardos, economista, enumera las tres características del Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez: “Desprecio a la rendición de cuentas”
articles.standfirst: El profesor de Economía critica la falta de asunción de responsabilidades políticas
articles.summary: El profesor de Economía critica la falta de asunción de responsabilidades políticas
articles.body: Gonzalo Bernardos ha publicado en su cuenta de X una crítica al funcionamiento del Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez en la que señala tres aspectos que considera característicos de su forma de actuar. El economista pone el foco en la falta de responsabilidades políticas, el desprecio a la rendición de cuentas y la utilización de la propaganda para proyectar una imagen de gestión que, según su valoración, no se corresponde con la realidad. En su publicación, Bernardos resume sus reproches en tres puntos. El primero es la “falta de asunción de responsabilidades políticas”, en referencia a la gestión del ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, al que considera que ha reaccionado “tarde y mal”. El segundo es el “desprecio a la rendición de cuentas”, una crítica a la falta de explicaciones y de reconocimiento de responsabilidades ante los problemas que afectan al Ejecutivo. El tercer aspecto que destaca es “la ocultación de la falta de gestión en propaganda, relato y vídeos de TikTok”. El economista considera que la comunicación del Gobierno ha adquirido un protagonismo que, en su opinión, sirve para tapar las deficiencias de su actuación política. Bernardos acompaña su mensaje con una publicación de El Confidencial titulada 'Desmontando el plan de Sánchez: no me gusta perder'. El economista considera que el accidente ferroviario de Urda ha cambiado el escenario de la campaña electoral. “Ha dado un vuelco a la campaña electoral”, sostiene, al entender que el suceso ha desplazado los mensajes emocionales dirigidos a los votantes y ha colocado la gestión en el centro del debate. Bernardos señala que esta nueva situación perjudica al PSOE porque, en su opinión, durante los últimos cuatro años la gestión no ha sido una prioridad para el partido. “Una situación que le va fatal al PSOE, pues en los últimos cuatro años no le ha interesado lo más mínimo”, afirma. El accidente ha situado así la actuación de los responsables políticos y la rendición de cuentas entre los asuntos que marcan la discusión electoral.

"Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high," he said (1).

Then he took aim at one of President Donald Trump's signature policies.

"Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long."

To show how far some Americans were being pushed, Cruz pointed to a growing share of workers forced to crack open their retirement savings.

"In 2025, 6% of 401(k) holders took hardship withdrawals, paying penalties. That is a record, and triple the norm," he said.

Cruz didn't name his source, but the figure matches Vanguard's How America Saves 2026 (2) report. Vanguard found that 6% of eligible participants in the plans it administers took at least one hardship withdrawal in 2025. That's up from 4.8% a year earlier and roughly triple the pre-pandemic average of about 2%.

Money you take out through a hardship withdrawal is money that can no longer grow in your retirement account. And there can be a cost up front, too.

A hardship withdrawal from a traditional 401(k) generally counts as taxable income. If you're under 59½, you may also owe an additional 10% tax unless you qualify for an exception. And unlike a 401(k) loan, a hardship withdrawal can't be paid back into the plan.

The strain Cruz described is showing up at the grocery checkout, too. In a LendingTree survey (3), 29% of buy now, pay later users said they had used the loans to buy groceries, more than double the 14% who said so two years earlier. Other than groceries, BNPL users have used these loans to pay for medical and dental care, and utility bills (4).

articles.title: Washington made Moscow a pariah. Now a tanker of Russian diesel is headed for US shores
articles.summary: When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the response from the United States and its allies was swift and brutal. The West launched an economic onslaught against the Kremlin, banning Russian imports, cutting Russia off from its payments systems and imposing a price cap on Russian oil sales to deplete the Kremlin’s coffers.
articles.body: When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the response from the United States and its allies was swift and brutal. The West launched an economic onslaught against the Kremlin, banning Russian imports, cutting Russia off from its payment systems and imposing a price cap on Russian oil sales to deplete the Kremlin’s coffers. Fast-forward to 2026, and the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes is carrying 300,000 barrels of Russian diesel toward the United States, offering a striking image of Washington’s about-face on Moscow. US President Donald Trump’s willingness to provide sanctions relief to Russia and cut business deals with President Vladimir Putin while war rages in Ukraine is chipping away at Russia’s status as an international pariah. It also undermines years-long efforts by the United States and its allies to punish and isolate the Russian economy in response to Putin’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor. In early 2022, “there was a very strong notion that we didn’t want a drop of Russian oil on US shores, not just from the US government but also industry,” said Ben Harris, who was closely involved in efforts to sanction Russia at the time as assistant Treasury Secretary. Trump’s actions signal that “he really sees no value in sanctioning Russia and he doesn’t see sanctions as a way to end the (Ukraine) war,” added Harris, now vice president and director of economic studies at the Brookings Institution. “It’s really unclear if he even sees Russian aggression as a problem,” he told CNN, describing Trump’s recent moves as “incredibly disheartening.” Trump’s controversial decision to buy diesel from Russia came weeks ahead of the midterm elections, when soaring fuel prices were a key pain point for voters. Diesel prices have surged above $6 a gallon for the first time ever, from $3.76 a gallon nationally before the Iran war. Average gasoline prices are above $4 a gallon, up from $3 a year ago, according to AAA data. Trump’s diesel purchases will do nothing to dent prices, however. The barrels on the Agioi Fanendes amount to roughly 10% of what the US transportation sector alone consumes each day, according to the Energy Information Administration. Even if all of Russia’s 2.2 million barrels were imported, in line with Trump’s plan, that would not be enough to supply America’s needs even for a single day. Pariah no more? Even so, the deal could be the first of several transactions between the United States and Russia, in what would amount to a stunning break from the past four years. These potential business deals — which reportedly range from Russia-US data center projects to joint liquified natural gas ventures in the Arctic — come despite the absence of a ceasefire in Ukraine and with no apparent conditions that would force an end to Russian aggression. The diesel deal might be the “first inkling” of this new approach, “which made people quite nervous because of what it might portend in the near future,” said Thomas Wright, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington, DC-based think tank. A deal on Russian oil major Lukoil’s international assets, led by a consortium that includes American investors, is expected within weeks, Reuters reported on Tuesday. It’s unclear how or whether the Democrat-controlled Congress could affect any current or future deals with Russia. But Trump still has veto power, which he could use to assert his authority on foreign policy. Before the midterms, the Trump administration and the Kremlin had discussed the possible lifting of US sanctions on Russia’s multibillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund. The Biden administration first imposed the sanctions in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, calling it a “known slush fund” for Putin and his inner circle. A US official said last week that the administration is undertaking its “normal process” in assessing sanctions relief for the fund, “in an effort to improve U.S.-Russia relations and help end the war.” In yet another sign of Trump’s conciliatory approach to Putin, Trump waived sanctions related to Russian fossil fuel sales days before they were due to take effect last month, sparking bipartisan backlash. The measures were included in the Graham Act, legislation named after Senator Lindsey Graham, a noted Russia hawk who died in July. The Graham Act would also have imposed tariffs on the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, including India. Instead, the diesel deal will make India and other buyers of Russian exports, including China, less fearful of repercussions, according to Elina Ribakova, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics and vice president for foreign policy at the Kyiv School of Economics. Trump’s diesel deal sends an “important signal,” she added. Buyer beware It remains to be seen whether the Agioi Fanendes will reach US shores. Two other sanctioned oil tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US have already been diverted, likely due to hesitancy from US buyers worried about legal consequences, said Matt Smith, Kpler’s director of commodity research. The Agioi Fanendes remains bound for the United States, “but has been slow in the last few days,” he told CNN. “This cargo is not guaranteed to discharge amid such uncertainty and may yet divert like the other two cargoes have done.” A Trump administration official told CNN Thursday that “consistent with the deal agreed to between President Trump and President Putin, Russian diesel is on the water and heading to the market, which will ease prices for Americans.” But New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, has warned the state’s port and terminal operators that importing Russian diesel violates federal law and could result in civil and criminal penalties. “New Jersey will not stand by while Donald Trump supports Vladimir Putin at the expense of Americans,” she said in a statement Monday. “Instead of lowering costs, he is helping finance Putin’s war against Ukraine and a global campaign of violence and terror that endangers U.S. service members abroad.” According to Harris of Brookings, the private sector is staying away from the Russian barrels. “You can’t find a buyer for Russian diesel,” he said. “What you’re seeing is the private sector has a different level of morality than the White House.” CNN’s Matt Egan, Jennifer Hansler, Farida Elsebai, Billy Stockwell and Phil Mattingly contributed reporting.

articles.title: 'E20 petrol by PSU firms meets prescribed quality standards': Oil ministry rejects Karnataka charge
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The petroleum ministry on Saturday rejected Karnataka's allegations of excessive ethanol content in petrol sold at some retail outlets, saying
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The petroleum ministry on Saturday rejected Karnataka's allegations of excessive ethanol content in petrol sold at some retail outlets, saying tests conducted by state-run oil companies found all 893 samples collected across 27 states and Union territories compliant with prescribed quality standards. The findings included 56 samples from Karnataka, which recorded ethanol content between 19 and 20 per cent.In a statement, the ministry said Indian Oil Corporation (IOC), Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL) tested the samples and found ethanol levels within the prescribed 19-21 per cent range under the Bureau of Indian Standards' IS 17021 specification. The Karnataka samples had an average ethanol content of 19.30 per cent, it added, news agency PTI reported.The findings contradict Karnataka's statement, which claimed that samples collected from certain fuel stations in October 2026 contained 26-31 per cent ethanol.The three oil marketing companies (OMCs) have questioned the state's sampling and testing procedures, saying the results cannot be independently verified without complete documentation and compliance with prescribed statutory procedures. They said they were not provided with retention samples, outlet-wise details or complete laboratory reports despite seeking them through the state level coordinator.The companies also flagged discrepancies in certificates issued by a third-party laboratory, arguing that the documents did not specify the test method, dilution procedure or reference material used to determine ethanol content through Gas Chromatography. They have sought access to counterpart samples for independent testing at an authorised laboratory in the presence of state officials and OMC representatives.The controversy comes amid concerns over the nationwide rollout of E20 petrol, which contains 20 per cent ethanol, including questions about vehicle mileage, engine compatibility and repair costs. The ministry said the impact on mileage varies according to vehicle category and engine calibration. Vehicles calibrated for E20 could see a reduction of around 1-2 per cent, while some other vehicles could experience a decline of 3-6 per cent.The OMCs have also disputed estimates that E20 could result in annual mileage losses worth Rs 62,000 crore and vehicle repair expenses of Rs 39,000 crore. They said applying a blanket assumption of 10 per cent mileage loss across all vehicles was not scientifically established and sought supporting performance data and repair-cost records.Defending the programme, the ministry cited its contribution to energy security, lower crude oil imports and agricultural incomes. Since the 2014-15 ethanol supply year, the initiative has resulted in foreign exchange savings of more than Rs 1.97 lakh crore, substitution of approximately 316 lakh metric tonnes of crude oil and payments exceeding Rs 1.66 lakh crore to farmers, according to ministry figures.The OMCs said more than 30 crore two-wheelers and four crore four-wheelers have been using E20 fuel for over three years, with no reported widespread vehicle breakdowns attributable to fuel quality. articles.title: Tech stocks are now cheaper than the S&P 500 for the first time since 2017 — here's what history says comes next: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Chip stocks lost nearly 30% in five weeks, but the typical S&P 500 stock barely moved, and tech now trades below the market's valuation for the first time si...
articles.body:
Wall Street partied the day after the midterms and woke up Thursday to tech's worst day since the 2020 COVID crash. Strip out the AI trade, though, and most stocks barely noticed.

The equal-weight S&P 500 ( RSP ), a stand-in for the typical stock, closed at a record Wednesday and ended the week within about 1% of where it started.

The headline indexes weren't so lucky. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) and Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) each fell about 3% for a fourth straight losing week, capping a week of whiplash that ended with a Friday bounce in chip stocks.

The selling did something few investors would have bet on a year ago. It made tech cheaper than the broader market.

Tech stocks in the S&P 500 ( XLK ) traded at about 17 times expected earnings this week, below the broader index's 18 times for the first time since 2017, Truist Wealth chief investment officer Keith Lerner wrote in a note Thursday. At the October 2025 peak, the sector fetched 32 times.

"At a 32.0x P/E last year, the market had baked in a lot of good news," Lerner wrote. "Arguably, at almost half that level, the market is already pricing in a lot of bad news."

Chips took the brunt of it. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) fell for a fifth straight week and lost nearly 30% over that stretch, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. Micron ( MU ) and Sandisk ( SNDK ) each lost more than 20% this week alone.

Lerner sees "something of a buyers' strike in tech," and he told Yahoo Finance Friday that chips are the first to feel any slowdown in data-center building, a risk that hung over the midterms . But a slower build-out could ease the cash drain on the biggest AI spenders.

"If this forces a little bit of a slowdown and maybe a little bit of positive in cash flow, I think that could actually elongate the cycle," he said.

Truist's advice is to stay overweight US large caps and add small caps "as a partial hedge against periodic sharp rotations away from megacap tech." The firm also notes that stocks have risen in the year after every midterm since 1946.

The S&P 500 has had 33 streaks of four or more losing weeks since 1990. Three months later, it was higher about 80% of the time, with a median gain of 6%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.

That's better than the typical three-month return of about 3% after any week.

The exceptions came during the dot-com bust and the 2008 financial crisis, when the S&P 500 kept falling for another year.

Michael Martin, founder of TraderMindset.com, isn't buying the dip. "It's a time to harvest cash right now," Martin, who runs a commodity futures strategy with Victor "Trader Vic" Sperandeo, told Yahoo Finance. "I don't think these are buying opportunities. Everything's in a downtrend."

articles.title: Wall Street Strategists Call Stock Rout a Fresh Reason to Buy
articles.summary: A slew of Wall Street strategists were banking on a short-term selloff following the US midterm elections to give investors an opportunity to buy stocks at a...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- A slew of Wall Street strategists were banking on a short-term selloff following the US midterm elections to give investors an opportunity to buy stocks at a discount.

On Thursday, they got far more than they bargained for. And now they're urging their clients to take advantage.

"This is the place where you should be adding risk over the next two to three weeks," said Mike Wilson, chief US equity strategist at Morgan Stanley.

Wilson was just as surprised as everyone else at the severity of the selling on Thursday that sent the S&P 500 Index down 4.4% and the Nasdaq 100 Index tumbling 6.4% due to concerns that newly empowered Democrats will slow the artificial intelligence build out.

Still, Wilson is confident that US stocks are poised for a rally, and he's sticking to his target for the S&P 500 to reach 8,000 by the end of the year, which would imply a gain of 8.4% from Friday's close.

Investors waded back into the market on Friday, sending the S&P 500 up 0.3%. But the benchmark is still down 2.5% since polls closed on Tuesday. Democrats won control of the Senate and House of Representatives, as well as numerous state houses and governor's mansions throughout the country. Many of the winning candidates pledged to check data center development and increase regulation.

The wipeout is evidence that the selloff in the S&P 500 in recent weeks is nearing an end, not a sign that the AI trade is collapsing, which would signal more pain ahead, Wilson and many of his Wall Street colleagues argue.

"We have had an AI bubble and I think the air is coming out of that bubble," Ed Yardeni, chief investment strategist at Yardeni Research, said in an interview on Thursday. "Bursting would mean that it would have significant adverse impacts on the economy, and I don't see that happening."

Wilson is recommending investors scoop up shares of consumer-focused stocks, particularly if interest rates and oil prices keep falling, while Yardeni likes healthcare stocks.

"I view it as a correction," said Yardeni, who has a year-end S&P 500 target of 7,900. "I anticipated buying opportunities after the elections, and I think we're starting to see some pretty good ones."

articles.title: Rolls-Royce's US chief says wealthy clients are 'quite protected' from market jitters
articles.summary: Rolls-Royce's well-heeled clients aren't pumping the brakes on new commissions, despite a choppy stock market and lingering economic worries, according to th...
articles.body:
Rolls-Royce's ( BMW.DE ) well-heeled clients aren't pumping the brakes on new commissions, despite a choppy stock market and lingering economic worries, according to the automaker's top executive in North America.

"Honestly, no," Nick Keen, president of Rolls-Royce Motor Cars North America, told Yahoo Finance at the Wynn Concours in Las Vegas when asked if clients are hesitating. "I think what we see is that our clients are quite protected from some of these instances."

Rather than money, the bigger concern for buyers is optics, Keen said.

"What we see is, is it the right time for me now, not financially, but is the perception of the right thing for me to be doing this at the moment," he said.

Rolls-Royce's long build times also help keep demand buoyant. Keen noted heavily personalized cars "can take a long time to be produced," giving the markets time "to right itself by the time it comes."

"For us in the US, we're seeing it still is fairly buoyant," said Keen, who took over the North American business on July 1 after joining the brand in 2015. "We're seeing sustainable growth."

Other regions are tougher for the British automaker. "The Middle East has been troubling at the moment because of what's been happening," Keen said, while China "remains an area that all of luxury is kind of struggling with."

Rolls-Royce doesn't break out US sales, but the Americas is its largest region. Globally, the BMW-owned brand delivered 5,664 cars in 2025 , down 0.8% year over year.

Not surprisingly, some regions are stronger than others. Keen called Florida "an enormous growth market," and said Rolls-Royce is taking its New York Private Office — its by-appointment bespoke studio — to the state for a weeklong "southern takeover" to court clients there. Florida's wealthy population has grown due to the state's lack of an income tax and the ability of many individuals to work from home.

In terms of products, the Cullinan SUV is Rolls-Royce's biggest seller in the US, with the electric Spectre coupe "a close second," according to Keen. Globally, the Cullinan made up 58% of deliveries last year, while Spectre sales fell 47%.

Keen said that drop in Spectre sales was planned. Rolls-Royce paused Spectre production ahead of the Series II update revealed in June , which brought more range, faster charging, and more power.

"That perceived slowdown was deliberate," he said, adding that orders and desirability have come "back straight away."

Keen admitted EV enthusiasm cooled as "infrastructure changed, regulations changed, and mindset changed a little bit." Rolls-Royce dropped its 2030 all-electric target in March. But the Spectre still sells because "it's a Rolls-Royce first, and an electric car second."
